questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a general-purpose random source fails for key material
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a general-purpose random source is unsafe for key material
questions.stem: A city planner's memo notes the depot access token generator draws its seed from the daily weather feed. What problem does that create for the tokens?

options.text: The seed is predictable to anyone who knows the weather, so tokens can be guessed
The tokens will be duplicated whenever the weather repeats, so access fails
options.misconception: confuses seed predictability with output duplication

options.text: The weather feed is too slow to generate tokens during a shift change
options.misconception: invents a performance problem the memo does not mention

options.text: Tokens from a weather source expire when the forecast is revised
options.misconception: invents an expiry rule that is not stated

questions.explanation: Key material must be unpredictable to an attacker, and a public forecast is known to anyone who cares to look. Because the seed determines every later output, guessing it lets an attacker predict tokens instead of searching for them.
questions.hint: Ask whether an outsider could reproduce the seed.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a repeated nonce costs under one key
questions.learningObjective: Explain the plaintext exposure caused by a repeated nonce
questions.stem: A memo records that the signal controller cipher used nonce value 7 on three separate nights under the same depot key. What does that pattern indicate?

options.text: The three nights produced identical ciphertexts for identical plaintexts
options.misconception: confuses nonce reuse with plaintext equality

options.text: The keystream was repeated, so plaintext from those nights can be recovered
The controller fell back to a weaker algorithm after the second night
options.misconception: invents an algorithm change not described

options.text: The depot key rotated automatically between the first and second night
options.misconception: invents a key rotation not described

questions.explanation: Reusing a nonce under one key reproduces the keystream, and two ciphertexts produced with the same keystream cancel it out, exposing the relationship between their plaintexts. The nonce must be unique per message under a given key, not merely repeated in a sensible-looking way.
questions.hint: Ask what happens when the keystream repeats.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What separates an initialisation vector from a key
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an initialisation vector from a key
questions.stem: In a council memo, an initialisation vector is described as a public, per-message value while the key stays in the depot safe. Which statement is right?

options.text: The vector is secret because it determines the whole ciphertext
options.misconception: confuses a public value with a secret one

options.text: The vector and the key are the same thing under two names
options.misconception: collapses two distinct values into one

options.text: The vector is public and per message, while the key is secret and reused
The vector replaces the key entirely in modern cipher modes
options.misconception: believes a public value can carry the secrecy

questions.explanation: An initialisation vector is not secret and is not reused in the way a key is; it is a per-message value that ensures identical plaintexts encrypt differently. The key is the secret material that must never be published, and a vector published alongside ciphertext is harmless on its own.
questions.hint: Ask which value must stay secret.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What the work factor in a key derivation is calibrated against
questions.learningObjective: Identify the weakness in a key derivation configured from a stale recommendation

stimulus.body: The depot access system derives its controller keys from a passphrase with an iteration count of 2,000. The supplier's current guidance recommends 600,000. The passphrase was written down when the depot opened in 2009 and has not been changed.

questions.stem: Given the memo extract, what is the main weakness in this key derivation setup?

options.text: The work factor is far too low for current hardware, and the passphrase is still guessable
The iteration count is too high, so officers cannot log in during a shift
options.misconception: assumes a low count slows logins rather than speeds attackers

options.text: The passphrase is too long, so key derivation cannot process it
options.misconception: treats length as a limitation rather than a strength

options.text: The salt must be removed, because a single salt slows down every login
options.misconception: believes salts work against attackers by slowing computation

questions.explanation: A work factor sets how much work an attacker must repeat per guess, and two thousand iterations is far below what current hardware can grind through. The known passphrase from 2009 is the other half of the problem, since a low factor only protects a secret that is actually secret.
questions.hint: Compare the setting against current hardware.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What an authenticated mode gives that plain encryption does not
questions.learningObjective: Plan the move from plain encryption to an authenticated mode
questions.stem: A memo describes the council's planning-file encryption as plain encryption with no tag. Choose the first change and the last change to make.

options.text: First: publish the keys; Last: use a longer passphrase for each file
options.misconception: publishes the very material that must stay secret

options.text: First: move to an authenticated mode; Last: verify the tag before releasing a file
First: increase the key length; Last: store the key in the same folder
options.misconception: lengthens the key but leaves files unauthenticated

options.text: First: compress the files before encrypting; Last: compress them again after
options.misconception: adds processing without adding any protection

questions.explanation: An authenticated mode adds a tag that proves the ciphertext was not altered and that the right key was used, which plain encryption cannot do. Verifying that tag before acting on a file is what turns a detected corruption into a blocked one.
questions.hint: Add integrity, then check it before trusting.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a message authentication code detects
questions.learningObjective: State what a message authentication code detects
questions.stem: A council memo describes a message authentication code attached to each planning instruction. What does that code detect?

options.text: Whether the message was sent by the person whose name is on it
options.misconception: treats a shared-secret tag as an identity proof

options.text: Whether the message content is factually correct
options.misconception: confuses integrity with accuracy

options.text: Whether the message was altered or was produced with a different key
Whether the message was sent at the time claimed in its header
options.misconception: assumes a tag carries trusted time

questions.explanation: A message authentication code lets a holder of the shared key detect any change to the message and detect a tag made under a different key. It says nothing about the truth of the content, the sender's identity, or the time, because all three need separate mechanisms.
questions.hint: Ask what changes the code would notice.

questions.topic: Why the order of encryption and authentication matters
questions.learningObjective: Compare the two orders of encryption and authentication
questions.stem: A memo compares two file-encryption procedures: encrypt-then-MAC and MAC-then-encrypt. Which statement about the pair is correct?

options.text: Encrypt-then-MAC is always weaker, since it checks the code after hiding it
options.misconception: assumes step order changes the maths rather than the risk

options.text: MAC-then-encrypt is always broken, so no protocol may use it
options.misconception: overstates a structural risk as universal failure

options.text: The two orders produce different ciphertext lengths for the same file
options.misconception: confuses ordering with encoding overhead

options.text: The order decides whether a failure is detected safely or exploited blindly

questions.explanation: Encrypting then authenticating lets the system reject a tampered ciphertext before decrypting, while authenticating then encrypting makes a padding check inside decryption reachable by an attacker. The order determines whether a bad input is refused or exploited.
questions.hint: Ask what the system does with a bad input.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a general-purpose random source fails for key material
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a general-purpose random source is unsafe for key material
questions.stem: A memo asks why the depot token generator cannot use the general-purpose random source the council already runs for survey draws. Explain it.

answer.exemplar: A general-purpose random source is tuned for statistical quality and speed, not for unpredictability under an adversary, and it may be seeded from an observable source such as process timing. Key material must be infeasible to predict or reconstruct, so it needs a cryptographically secure source, a proper seed, and the operational controls that keep the generated values out of logs.

questions.explanation: Key material has to resist an adversary who can observe the system and try to reconstruct the sequence. A source designed for fair draws can be predictable or reseeded predictably, and that difference is what makes it unusable for keys.
questions.hint: Unpredictability under an adversary is the requirement.

questions.topic: What a repeated nonce costs under one key
questions.learningObjective: Compute the plaintext exposure created by a reused nonce
questions.stem: A cipher under one key encrypts two different 16-byte messages with the same nonce. XORing the two ciphertexts cancels the keystream and reveals the XOR of the two plaintexts. How many bytes of plaintext relationship does that expose?
questions.explanation: Reusing the nonce repeats the keystream, so XORing the two ciphertexts cancels it and leaves the XOR of the two plaintexts across all 16 bytes. That is 16 bytes of relationship leaked, enough to read common structures and to recover plaintext once any part is guessed.
questions.hint: The keystream cancels across the whole block.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What separates an initialisation vector from a key
questions.learningObjective: Assess a vector and key arrangement described in a memo

stimulus.body: For the depot file cabinet, the current procedure takes a fresh 16-byte initialisation vector for each encrypted file and writes it in the clear at the front of the file. The 32-byte key is generated once and held on a card in the safe. Last month the same 16-byte vector was pasted into two files by mistake.

questions.stem: Given the memo extract, which statement best describes the position?

options.text: Publishing the vector in the clear compromises the key
options.misconception: believes public material breaks the key

options.text: The key stays secret, but the repeated vector exposes the plaintext relationship
The repeated vector means both files decrypt to the same plaintext
options.misconception: assumes same vector implies same ciphertext

options.text: The procedure is sound, because the key was generated only once
options.misconception: misses that the nonce, not the key, was mishandled

questions.explanation: A vector in the clear is expected and harmless; what matters is that it is unique per message under the key. Reusing it twice repeats the keystream, so the two files leak the relationship between their plaintexts while the key itself stays safe.
questions.hint: Look at what was repeated, not what was published.

questions.learningObjective: Choose the steps for adding a correctly salted account
questions.stem: A council portal hashes citizen passwords with a per-record salt. Choose the first step when adding a new account and the last step before the entry is trusted.

options.text: First: reuse the last account's salt; Last: store the hash in the log file
options.misconception: reuses salts and leaks the hash

options.text: First: generate a random salt; Last: hash the password without the salt
options.misconception: generates a salt and then ignores it

options.text: First: store the salt in the plaintext backup; Last: hash it again with a second salt
options.misconception: chains salts and stores them carelessly

options.text: First: generate a fresh random salt; Last: store it with the hash and the cost

questions.explanation: A fresh random salt per record is what stops identical passwords producing identical stored values and defeats precomputed tables. The salt has to be stored alongside the hash, because the verifier needs it to recompute the value, and the derivation cost has to be recorded so it can be raised later.
questions.hint: Fresh salt, stored with the hash and its cost.

questions.topic: What the work factor in a key derivation is calibrated against
questions.learningObjective: State what a key derivation work factor is calibrated against
questions.stem: A memo asks what the work factor in a key derivation function is calibrated against. Which answer is right?

options.text: The guessing effort an attacker is expected to have to make per candidate secret
The number of files that can be encrypted before the key must change
options.misconception: confuses cost with key lifetime

options.text: The number of seconds a legitimate officer is willing to wait at a terminal
options.misconception: describes a user tolerance rather than the attack cost

options.text: The memory footprint the council's servers are permitted to use
options.misconception: describes a resource limit rather than the attack cost

questions.explanation: The work factor is chosen so that each guess by an attacker is expensive while a legitimate derivation stays fast enough to use. It is a calibration against the attacker's effort and available hardware, not against key lifetime, user patience or server memory.

questions.stem: A memo records that the council's file cipher is unauthenticated, that 4,000 planning files are stored in it, and that each file's contents are checked by hand before issue. What does this combination imply?

options.text: The hand checks make the lack of authentication harmless
options.misconception: assumes a manual step removes the need for one

options.text: Detection depends on a human reading the file, so the cipher itself provides none
All 4,000 files are exposed, since unauthenticated encryption fails for every file
options.misconception: equates a missing tag with a broken cipher

options.text: The 4,000 file count shows the risk is concentrated in large volumes
options.misconception: reads a count as a severity measure

Files that are never opened by eye carry no such detection, so the protection is partial and depends on the reading step rather than the cipher.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a message authentication code detects
questions.learningObjective: Describe the limits of a message authentication code
questions.stem: A memo proposes using a message authentication code to protect planning instructions. Explain what it will and will not tell the planner.

answer.exemplar: The code will tell the planner that the instruction has not been altered since it was tagged and that it was produced under the shared key, so a tampered or forged instruction is rejected on receipt. It will not tell them that the content is true, that the sender was a particular person, or that the message is recent, because each of those needs a separate mechanism such as a signature, a review step or trusted time.

questions.explanation: A message authentication code is a shared secret mechanism that detects change and key mismatch, and nothing more. Convincing a reader that the content is true or who sent it requires evidence the code cannot supply.
questions.hint: Integrity is what the code provides.

questions.topic: Why a general-purpose random source fails for key material
questions.learningObjective: Identify the risk in a seeded random source used for tokens

stimulus.body: The survey system's random source is a library routine seeded once at start of day with the current time in milliseconds. The seed is logged in the system log for debugging. Tokens issued by the routine are used as depot keypad codes for the day.

questions.stem: Given the memo extract, what is the risk to the keypad codes?

options.text: Anyone who reads the log can predict the day's codes and enter the depot
The codes will repeat if two routines start within the same millisecond
options.misconception: confuses a predictable seed with duplicate outputs

options.text: The library routine cannot produce codes fast enough for a morning shift
options.misconception: invents a throughput problem the extract does not mention

options.text: The codes will stop working when the system clock is adjusted
options.misconception: invents a clock dependency the extract does not state

questions.explanation: The seed is derived from a value anyone can read from the log, and everything the routine produces follows from that seed. Predicting the seed lets an attacker compute the day's codes directly, which is far cheaper than testing codes one by one.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a repeated nonce costs under one key
questions.learningObjective: Choose the steps that restore nonce uniqueness across key changes
questions.stem: A council system encrypts nightly traffic reports with one key and a counter that resets at midnight. Choose the first fix and the last check.

options.text: First: rotate the key at midnight; Last: keep the old counter values for the new key
options.misconception: rotates the key while keeping the colliding values

options.text: First: make the counter unique across every key; Last: verify no counter repeats ever
First: change the cipher; Last: test the new cipher with the same counters
options.misconception: changes the algorithm but keeps the colliding inputs

options.text: First: shorten the counter; Last: log every counter used for a week
options.misconception: shortens the space where the collision already sits

questions.explanation: A counter reset under one key makes two messages share a nonce, which repeats the keystream and leaks plaintext relationships. The fix is to guarantee uniqueness across all keys that ever touch the data, and the check is to prove that no counter value has ever been reused.
questions.hint: Uniqueness has to hold across every key.

options.misconception: judges secrecy by length alone

options.text: The key changes for every file while the vector stays the same
options.misconception: swaps the two roles of key and vector

The two values are interchangeable, since either one can start the cipher

questions.topic: What a salt has to be unique per record for
questions.learningObjective: Explain why one salt across many records weakens password storage
questions.stem: A portal audit finds that 12 of 500 citizen accounts produce the same stored hash value, and the account creation log shows the same salt recorded for all 12. What does this show?

options.text: Those 12 citizens share a password, so the risk is a weak shared secret
options.misconception: assumes equal hashes mean equal passwords

options.text: The portal's hashing is broken, because equal hashes are impossible
options.misconception: denies a basic property of hashing

options.text: The 12 accounts were created by the same person
options.misconception: infers identity from a hash collision pattern

options.text: The shared salt lets one precomputed table attack many accounts at once

questions.explanation: When one salt covers many records, an attacker can hash each candidate password once against that salt and then search for the resulting values across all the accounts. Per-record salts remove that single-table advantage and also separate accounts that share a password.
questions.hint: One salt for many records means one table for many records.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What the work factor in a key derivation is calibrated against
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a work factor increase in terms of attacker cost
questions.stem: A memo notes that raising a derivation cost from 2,000 to 600,000 slows the depot's logon from 0.4 seconds to 1.1 seconds. Explain how to read this.

answer.exemplar: The slowdown is the cost of the protection: the number of iterations sets how much work each guess costs an attacker, so it should be set high enough that guessing a passphrase is impractical on current hardware. The legitimate user pays a fraction of a second, while an attacker trying many candidates pays the same cost thousands of times over, which is the asymmetry the setting is designed to create.

questions.explanation: A work factor is only meaningful in comparison to the attacker's budget, so a low figure that is comfortable for a user is also comfortable for an attacker. The correct comparison is not the logon delay alone but how many guesses that delay buys the attacker.
questions.hint: Compare the user's delay with the attacker's budget.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a message authentication code detects
questions.learningObjective: Find the structural weakness in a shared-key tag arrangement

stimulus.body: Site instructions sent to the depot tablet carry a 32-bit authentication tag. The tag is checked on arrival, and the tablet raises an alarm if the check fails. The tag is generated by a device that shares a single secret with all 40 tablets, and the same secret is used for every device in the estate.

questions.stem: Given the memo extract, what is the weakest point in this arrangement?

options.text: The alarm text is too vague to help the depot staff respond
options.misconception: criticises wording rather than the security design

options.text: A 32-bit tag is far too short for the volume of traffic
options.misconception: objects to a tag size that is adequate for its purpose

options.text: One shared secret means any compromised tablet can forge instructions for all
Checking tags on arrival is later than it should be
options.misconception: objects to the timing rather than the key sharing

questions.explanation: A single secret shared across 40 devices means every device can create valid tags for every other device, so one compromised tablet becomes a path to forging instructions estate-wide. A 32-bit tag and an arrival-time check are both reasonable; the shared key is the structural weakness.

options.misconception: adds key sprawl without removing the oracle

options.misconception: invented a key length problem

The nonce is longer than the message, so it dominates the ciphertext

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What separates an initialisation vector from a key
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a vector may be published but a key may not
questions.stem: A memo asks why a per-file vector may be published but the key may not. Explain the difference in terms of what each one controls.

answer.exemplar: The vector is an input to the cipher that removes the need for the key to stay secret, and its only job is to make two identical files encrypt differently, so publishing it costs nothing an attacker can use. The key is the secret that makes the ciphertext unreadable, so publishing it would let anyone decrypt every file ever protected with it, which is why the key lives in the safe and the vector sits in the file header.

questions.explanation: Publishing a value that only removes a weakness and protects no secrecy is harmless, while publishing the value that provides all the secrecy destroys it. The distinction is which value an attacker would need in order to read the data.
questions.hint: Ask which value an attacker needs to decrypt.

questions.stem: A portal hashes passwords with a per-account salt. An attacker wants to test one candidate password against all 500 accounts. How many hash computations does that single candidate require with per-account salts?
questions.explanation: Per-account salts force the candidate to be hashed once for every account, so one candidate costs 500 computations instead of one. With a shared salt the same 500 accounts would be covered by a single precomputed value, which is the advantage unique salts exist to remove.
questions.hint: Each record needs its own computation.

The codes change too often, which slows technicians during faults

options.misconception: prescribes a fix without identifying the weakness

options.misconception: raises a logging point while the guessing risk stays

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a general-purpose random source fails for key material
questions.learningObjective: Write the justification for adopting a cryptographically secure source
questions.stem: A memo asks the depot to justify moving from the general-purpose random source to a cryptographically secure one for key material. Write the justification.

answer.exemplar: The general-purpose source is built to produce fair-looking numbers for draws and statistics, and it may be seeded from an observable value such as the clock or a process id, both of which an attacker can guess. Key material must resist reconstruction by someone who can observe the system, so the justification is that a secure source is designed for that threat, that its seed is handled as secret, and that the values never reach logs or backups.

questions.explanation: The justification has to be about the threat model rather than about the appearance of randomness. A source designed for draws can be reconstructed by an observer, so key material needs one built for adversarial unpredictability and a seed handled accordingly.
questions.hint: Argue from the threat model, not from looks.

options.text: Service A, because a fresh vector each time wastes randomness
options.misconception: objects to correctness

options.text: Neither, because both vectors are stored with the ciphertext
options.misconception: ignores the reuse issue because the vector is public

options.text: Service B, because a reused vector repeats the keystream for every file
Service B, because storing the vector publicly leaks the key
options.misconception: confuses a public input with the secret

options.misconception: cannot re-hash a hash without the password

options.text: First: replace all salts with one new salt; Last: hash the new values
options.misconception: collapses the salts that were the point

options.text: First: raise the work factor; Last: leave the stored values untouched
options.misconception: raises the cost but changes nothing already stored

options.text: First: generate a fresh salt per account; Last: re-derive each value from the password

options.text: The key must have been broken, since altered files were found
options.misconception: assumes tampering implies key compromise

options.text: Without authentication, alteration is only caught by chance or by routine inspection
Six altered files prove the cipher provides no confidentiality
options.misconception: confuses integrity with confidentiality

options.text: The archive should be re-encrypted with a different key per file
options.misconception: prescribes a fix without the diagnosis

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a message authentication code detects
questions.learningObjective: Argue against a single estate-wide authentication code
questions.stem: A memo proposes replacing per-device authentication codes with one estate-wide code. Write the argument the depot should make.

answer.exemplar: One estate-wide code concentrates trust in a single value, so every device that holds it can produce tags accepted by all the others, and one lost or borrowed device exposes the whole estate. Per-device codes limit the blast radius to a single site, make revocation local when a device is lost, and give the depot an accurate answer about which device sent a given instruction.

questions.explanation: The argument is about blast radius and revocation rather than about tidiness. A single shared code turns any single compromise into an estate-wide forgery capability, and it makes an accurate question about the source of a message impossible to answer.
questions.hint: Argue from blast radius and revocation.

options.text: The key is derived from a guessable public input, so a session can be reproduced
The hash function is broken, because it produced a collision
options.misconception: misreads a normal coincidence as a hash failure

options.text: The portal should store keys hashed rather than in plaintext
options.misconception: prescribes storage practice as the root cause

options.text: Reference numbers should be longer to reduce collisions
options.misconception: treats length as a fix for derivation weakness

questions.explanation: The key comes from material the applicant and the public both know, so anyone who can guess a reference can reproduce that applicant's session key. The collision is a symptom of the same weakness, not a separate flaw in the hash.

questions.topic: What a repeated nonce costs under one key
questions.learningObjective: Choose the design that guarantees nonce uniqueness over years
questions.stem: Choose the first step and the last step for guaranteeing nonce uniqueness in a service that encrypts under one key for years.

options.text: First: generate a random nonce each time; Last: check the log for duplicates
options.misconception: relies on randomness that cannot be verified exhaustively

options.text: First: use a counter that never repeats; Last: persist and verify the counter state
First: rotate the key every month; Last: accept the rare duplicate nonce
options.misconception: leaves duplicates and adds key churn

options.text: First: derive the nonce from the timestamp; Last: assume the clock never repeats
options.misconception: trusts a clock as the uniqueness source

questions.explanation: A counter gives uniqueness by construction, and the counter state has to be persisted and checked so a restart cannot silently reuse values. Random or time-based nonces leave a small collision chance that grows over years, which is why a counter with durable state is the dependable choice.
questions.hint: Uniqueness by construction, with durable state.

options.misconception: reverses the roles of key and vector

options.text: The vectors must be rotated because they are published alongside files
options.misconception: assumes publication forces rotation

options.text: The master key must be protected, while vectors may be stored openly
Both must be protected equally, because both feed the cipher
options.misconception: ignores that only one carries secrecy

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a general-purpose random source fails for key material
questions.learningObjective: Write the requirements paragraph for key material generation
questions.stem: A memo asks the depot to state in one paragraph why its key material must come from a source built for adversarial unpredictability. Write the paragraph.

answer.exemplar: Key material is only as strong as the process that produced it, so the council needs a source designed for attackers who can observe the machine and try to reconstruct its output, not one designed to produce fair-looking numbers for surveys and draws. The source must be seeded unpredictably, the seed must be protected, and generated values must never appear in logs, backups or printouts, because every copy is another chance for the sequence to be recovered.

questions.explanation: The paragraph has to name the adversary, the seeding and the handling of the outputs, since each is a separate link in the chain. A paragraph that only says the source is cryptographically secure leaves the operational half of the problem open.
questions.hint: Cover the source, the seed and the handling.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a repeated nonce costs under one key
questions.learningObjective: Compute the plaintext volume affected by one nonce mistake
questions.stem: A memo says one depot key encrypts 500 nightly traffic reports of 2,000 bytes each, and that one nonce was used twice by mistake. How many bytes of plaintext were encrypted under a keystream that was used twice?
questions.explanation: The mistake affected two reports of two thousand bytes each, so four thousand bytes of plaintext were encrypted under a keystream that was used twice. The key itself is unaffected, but the relationship between those two reports is exposed and cannot be repaired by re-encrypting them later.
questions.hint: Two reports share one keystream.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What separates an initialisation vector from a key
questions.learningObjective: Recognise the behaviour a fresh vector produces

stimulus.body: The depot file service writes the initialisation vector in the first 16 bytes of every encrypted file, in the clear. Two files of exactly the same size and content were uploaded on the same morning and produced different ciphertexts. The service's key is 32 bytes and has not been changed since 2021.

questions.stem: Given the memo extract, which observation confirms the service is behaving correctly?

options.text: The key has stayed the same since 2021, which proves the vectors are fresh
options.misconception: infers freshness from an unrelated fact

options.text: The vector appears in clear text, so the ciphertext is only partly secret
options.misconception: treats a public input as a weakness

options.text: Identical files produced different ciphertexts, which is what a fresh vector achieves
Both files are the same size, so the service must have reused the vector
options.misconception: draws an unrelated inference from file size

questions.explanation: Different ciphertexts for identical content is exactly what a per-file vector is supposed to deliver, since it stops an observer spotting repeated files. The published vector and the unchanged key are both expected and unremarkable, so the differing ciphertexts are the informative observation.
questions.hint: Look for the effect the vector is designed to produce.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a salt has to be unique per record for
questions.learningObjective: Choose the steps for storing salted password hashes
questions.stem: Choose the first step and the last step for storing salted password hashes in a new council system.

options.text: First: pick one salt for the whole system; Last: store it next to the hashes
options.misconception: collapses the protection that per-record salts provide

options.text: First: hash the password with the salt; Last: store the salt in a separate table
options.misconception: stores the salt separately without reason

options.text: First: store the password so it can be re-hashed later; Last: remove the plaintext
options.misconception: keeps the very secret that hashing exists to remove

options.text: First: generate a unique random salt per record; Last: store the salt with the hash

questions.explanation: A unique random salt per record is what makes identical passwords produce different stored values and defeats precomputed tables. The salt must be stored alongside the hash, since the verifier needs it to recompute the value, and the derivation cost should be recorded so it can be raised when hardware improves.
questions.hint: Unique salt per record, kept with the hash.
